questions.question: What equation defines an idempotent matrix A?
Why must the matrix be square for idempotence?
options: The transpose is defined only for square matrices.
Only square matrices can have zero entries.
Only square matrices can be multiplied by vectors.
$A^2$ must be a meaningful matrix product of A with itself.

questions.question: What is the interpretation of applying an idempotent matrix twice?
options: The second application always gives zero.
The second application reverses the first.
The second application changes nothing beyond the first.
The second application always gives the identity.

questions.question: Which two standard matrices are always idempotent?
options: Every singular matrix and every symmetric matrix.
The zero square matrix and the identity matrix.
Every invertible matrix and every permutation matrix.
Every diagonal matrix and every triangular matrix.

questions.question: If an idempotent matrix is invertible, what must it be?
Is $I_3$ idempotent?
options: Only if the field is complex.
No, because the identity matrix is invertible.
No, because idempotent matrices must be zero.

questions.question: Is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ idempotent?
options: Only if the vector space is one-dimensional.
No. Its square is the identity.
No. Its square is the zero matrix.

questions.question: Is the zero $2\times2$ matrix idempotent?
options: No, because it has no inverse.

questions.question: Is $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ idempotent?
options: No, because diagonal matrices cannot be idempotent.

questions.question: If $P^2=P$, what is $P^3$?
Why are projection matrices natural examples of idempotent matrices?
options: Projecting twice always gives the zero vector.
Projecting twice gives the same result as projecting once.
Projection matrices are always invertible but not identity.

questions.question: Can an idempotent matrix be singular?
options: Only if it is also the identity.
Yes. The zero matrix and nontrivial projections are singular examples.
No. Singular matrices cannot be squared.
No. Idempotent matrices are always invertible, in every case without exception.

questions.question: What eigenvalues can an idempotent matrix have?
Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. What is $P(0,5)^T$?
For the same $P$, what is $P(P(3,4)^T)$?
Suppose an idempotent matrix A is invertible. Starting from $A^2=A$, what do you get after multiplying on the left by $A^{-1}$?
Why does $A^2=A$ suggest a decomposition into fixed and killed directions?
options: Eigenvalues must satisfy $λ^2=λ$, so only λ=1 and λ=0 can occur.
Every vector is sent to a new independent vector.
The matrix must have no eigenvectors.

questions.question: If an idempotent matrix is not the identity, what must be true if it is invertible?
options: It must be a nontrivial Jordan block linear-algebra condition.
It must be the zero matrix.
That situation cannot happen. An invertible idempotent matrix must be identity.

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Is A idempotent?
options: Only if the off-diagonal entry is 0.
No, because its square is zero.
No, because it is not diagonal.
